Bringing Irish whiskey and Japanese music culture together

As The Busker Irish Whiskey expanded into Japan, the opportunity was to build meaningful connections between the drinks brand and the local music scene. We set out to create a culturally relevant platform that brought The Busker's 'Whiskey Made for Music' proposition to life through authentic partnerships with Japanese artists and venues.

What if a whiskey brand could become part of the local music scene by giving its artists a platform to shine? We brought together The Busker's distinctive Triple Cask, Triple Smooth story with Japan's thriving live music culture, creating a partnership that celebrated local talent while introducing new audiences to the brand.

The strongest brand partnerships create value on both sides. By collaborating with local artists and venues, The Busker could contribute to Japan’s music culture while building brand awareness, encouraging product discovery and creating experiences that resonated with audiences both inside and beyond the venue.

We collaborated with Japanese artists including singer-songwriter luvis and multi-instrumentalist TENDRE, hosting intimate performances at Tokyo's Music Bar Cave in Shibuya, with a third session planned for Osaka.

Great brand experiences become part of the culture they’re entering. By embracing Japan’s local music scene and turning The Busker’s product story into a creative format, Triple Sessions showed how curiosity can help brands connect with new audiences in meaningful ways.

The Busker Irish Whiskey launches ‘Triple Sessions’ in Japan via Curious Nation – Campaign Brief Asia
Australian and New Zealand brand activation agency Curious Nation has partnered with The Busker Irish Whiskey to bring its ‘Whiskey Made for Music’ proposition to life in Japan.

The Busker Irish Whiskey, produced at Royal Oak Distillery in County Carlow, Ireland, has strengthened its investment in Japan as a strategic growth market, launching ‘The Busker Triple Sessions’, a culturally-led music platform that brings the brand’s proposition to life through live performance, immersive experiences and a content first approach.

Curious Nation worked with client Disaronno International, in partnership with Japanese distributor Whisk-e, for The Busker Triple Sessions. Developed specifically for the Japanese market, it blends local music culture with The Busker’s triple cask story to build brand awareness, product trial and long term consumer affinity.

Rather than importing a global music artist, The Busker Triple Sessions has been built around Japan’s thriving live music scene and popular whiskey culture, collaborating with local artists and venues to create an authenticity that resonates with consumers.

Curious Nation led strategy, creative development, event design and production, content strategy, design and production, social media ecosystem development and end to end campaign delivery in Japan. While Massive Music partnered with Curious Nation on talent and licensing engagement.

The campaign launched at Tokyo’s renowned Music Bar Cave in Shibuya featuring Japanese singer-songwriter, luvis. Selection for the Japanese national team for international competitions used to center on breaking a "standard record." If you could just hit that mark, you could become a representative after going through the subsequent selection process. I myself continued to compete with that standard record as my goal.

In terms of the triple jump, the records of Japan's top athletes are between 16m50 and under 17m. Consistently hitting this mark of around 16m50 in five meets a year is the foundation for raising your ranking.

University track meets are the lowest F-rank, and even if you take first place, the points added are only about 10. As the rank goes up, the added points increase, but even the Japan Championships only reach B-rank, and the Grand Prix series only goes up to C-rank at best.

If you participate in all the high-ranking meets in Japan and post records, you can earn a certain amount of points. However, the reality is that the number of high-ranking meets themselves is overwhelmingly higher overseas.

Due to the evolution of spikes and tracks, as well as the development of training methods, records continue to improve globally. The environment where one can receive high-quality training from a young age has also expanded. However, this is not just a story about Japanese athletes; athletes around the world are in the same conditions.

Of course, this does not apply to an outstanding athlete who can jump 17m five times a year. However, for many athletes, in order to become a Japanese representative, an environment where they can continue to stand on the stage to compete with the world is essential first.

What does it take to compete on the world stage in the triple jump now?
For the first time in a while, I did a broadcast on stand.fm.
The theme was "The environment for triple jumpers." I have rewritten the content I talked about on the radio into an article.

Selection for the Japanese national team for international competitions used to center on breaking a "standard record." If you could just hit that mark, you could become a representative after going through the subsequent selection process. I myself continued to compete with that standard record as my goal.

However, around 2018, World Athletics introduced a ranking system. Currently, the average of the records from your top five meets over the course of a year becomes your points, and the system determines representatives based on that world ranking.

In terms of the triple jump, the records of Japan's top athletes are between 16m50 and under 17m. Consistently hitting this mark of around 16m50 in five meets a year is the foundation for raising your ranking.
